passages.original: Immo ex Augustini verbis in breviculo collationis cum Donatistis, cap. 18. intelligitur, Donatistas in collatione Carthaginensi primum id criminis Melchiadi imposuisse. « Cum enim eos compulisset Cognitor, » inquit Augustinus, « ut contra concilium judiciumque Melchiadis, quo Cæcilianus purgatus atque absolutus legebatur, si haberent aliquid, dicerent ; tunc Donatistae ipsum Melchiadem coeperunt traditionis arguere, et dicere majores suos propterea illius judicium refugisse. » Istud affirmantes mendacii convincere difficile admodum non erat: siquidem majores illorum Melchiadis judicio stare detrectantes, nihil umquam hujusmodi in precibus suis prætexuisse deprehenduntur.
passages.english: Indeed, from Augustine's words in the Summary of the Conference with the Donatists, chapter 18, it is understood that the Donatists first laid this charge against Melchiades at the Conference of Carthage. "For when the Commissioner had compelled them," says Augustine, "to state whatever they had, if they had anything, against the council and judgment of Melchiades, in which Caecilian was read to have been cleared and acquitted, then the Donatists began to accuse Melchiades himself of betrayal [of the scriptures], and to say that their predecessors had for that reason shunned his judgment." It was not at all difficult to convict those who asserted this of a lie, since their predecessors, when they refused to abide by the judgment of Melchiades, are found never to have put forward anything of this kind as a pretext in their petitions.
passages.notes: "traditionis": the crime of being a traditor, i.e. handing over the scriptures during persecution. "Cognitor": the imperial commissioner presiding at the Conference of Carthage (411).

passages.original: His religiosior Constantinus eorum appellationem molestissime tulit : sed paulo indulgentior quam par esset, dum audaciam non comprimit, gravibus Ecclesiæ malis locum et occasionem praebuit. Quamvis autem appellantibus aliud Arelatense judicium de- derit, hoc tamen, teste Augustino, epist. 43, olim 162, n. 20, dedit, « non quia jam necesse erat, sed eorum perversitatibus cedens, et omni modo cupiens tantam impudentiam cohibere. »Nec prohibuit hujusmodi appellatio, quominus, uHi jam exposuimus , episcopi Eunomius et Olympius, in Africam procomponendis Carlhaginensis ecclesiae rebus missi, postmodum pronuntiarint, sententiam decem et novem episcoporum jam dudum datam dissolvi non posse » (Optat., lib.
passages.english: Constantine, more religious than they, took their appeal very badly; but, being somewhat more indulgent than was proper, in not suppressing their audacity he gave room and occasion to grave evils for the Church. And although he granted the appellants another judgment, at Arles, he nevertheless granted this, as Augustine testifies (Letter 43, formerly 162, n. 20), "not because it was now necessary, but yielding to their perversities and wishing in every way to restrain such great impudence."
